summary.text: A chemical bond is an attraction that holds atoms or ions together in molecules, crystals and other structures.
Bonds come as ionic (charged ions attracting), covalent (shared electrons), metallic, or a mix, and they come from how the outer electrons of atoms behave.
Which kind of bond holds a material together decides its structure and properties, such as how strong, soft or brittle it is.

facts.label: Three strong types
facts.value: Covalent, ionic and metallic bonds are the strong, primary bonds

facts.label: Weak bond examples
facts.value: Hydrogen bonds and the London dispersion force are weak, secondary bonds

facts.label: Why ionic crystals crack
facts.value: Forces between ions are short-range, so cracks are not bridged

facts.label: Metal electron sea
facts.value: Each metal atom donates electrons to a shared sea between atoms

facts.label: Network covalent solids
facts.value: Diamond and quartz are covalent bonds extending through a whole solid

items.prompt: You drop a lump of table salt and it shatters instead of bending. What best explains this?

options.label: Its ions attract only at short range, so a crack is not bridged
Its electrons roam freely between all the atoms in the lump
Its bonds are weak and break at the slightest push of force
Its atoms share pairs of electrons along fixed chains in space

items.explain: Ionic bonds are strong but brittle because the forces between ions are short-range and do not bridge cracks.

items.prompt: A blacksmith hammers a bar of metal flat and it does not snap. Which bonding idea explains why?

options.label: Ions locked in place, each attracting only its nearest neighbours
Shared electrons forming a few fixed lines between pairs of atoms
Electrons in a shared sea, with atoms not attracted in set directions
Weak attractions between separate small molecules in the metal

items.explain: Metallic bonding is collective and not oriented in particular directions, so metal crystals deform more easily, which gives malleability.

items.prompt: Candle wax is soft and melts at a low temperature, yet it is built from covalently bonded molecules. Why?

options.label: The covalent bonds inside each molecule are very weak
The forces holding one molecule to the next are much weaker
The molecules are held together by a sea of electrons
The molecules are made of oppositely charged ions

items.explain: Covalent bonds make small molecules, and the weak intermolecular forces between them give waxes and oils their soft bulk and low melting points.

items.prompt: A diamond is far harder and has a much higher melting point than a wax candle. Both rely on covalent bonds. What is the difference?

options.label: Diamond's covalent bonds extend in a network through the whole solid
Diamond is held together by ions of opposite charge instead
Diamond has no bonds between its atoms, only loose contact
Diamond's bonds are weaker but there are simply more of them

items.explain: Covalent bonds that extend in networks through a solid, as in diamond, give strong, tough structures with high melting points, unlike small separate molecules.

items.prompt: A chemist finds a bond that is partly sharing and partly attraction between charges. What should she conclude about the types of bond?

options.label: The sample must be contaminated, since bonds are always one pure type
Only metals can show a mixture like this in practice
The bond must be a weak, secondary bond of some kind
Types of bond merge into each other, with no clear line between them

items.explain: The behaviours of valence electrons merge into each other, so no clear line separates the bond types, though the labels remain useful.

items.prompt: In a simple picture of an ionic bond, what happens to the bonding electron?

options.label: It is passed from one atom to the other, leaving opposite charges
It is shared equally between the two nuclei in the middle
It joins a sea of electrons spread over many atoms
It is lost entirely and no longer affects either atom

items.explain: The electron is transferred, so one atom becomes positive and the other negative, and their electrostatic attraction forms the bond.

right.label: Electrons donated to a shared sea

beats.prompt: One step in this reasoning about metals is wrong; which?

steps.text: Each metal atom donates electrons to a shared sea.
The electrons are free to be associated with many atoms at once.
So every bond points in one fixed direction between two atoms.
So metal crystals can deform more easily, giving malleability.

beats.idea: The way atoms are held together, by transfer, sharing or a sea of electrons, decides how a material breaks, bends or melts.

paragraphs.heading: What a bond is
paragraphs.text: A chemical bond is an attraction between atoms. It is what lets atoms or ions join up into molecules, crystals and other structures. Bonds hold together the atoms of molecules, crystals, metals and other forms of matter, and the bonds decide how the material is built and how it behaves. The differences between kinds of bond come from how the outermost electrons of the atoms, called valence electrons, behave.

paragraphs.heading: Strong and weak bonds
paragraphs.text: A bond can come from the pull between ions of opposite charge, which makes an ionic bond, from atoms sharing electrons, which makes a covalent bond, or from a mix of both. Chemists also sort bonds by strength. Covalent, ionic and metallic bonds count as strong or primary bonds. Hydrogen bonds, the London dispersion force and dipole–dipole interactions count as weak or secondary ones. The kinds shade into each other with no clear border, yet naming them separately is still useful, since they give materials different properties.

paragraphs.heading: Why atoms stick together
paragraphs.text: Opposite charges attract, so the negative electrons around an atom and the positive protons in its nucleus pull on each other. An electron shared by two nuclei is pulled by both of them. Bonded nuclei settle at a best spacing, the bond distance, where attraction and repulsion balance. Forming a bond releases energy. This is not because potential energy drops, since the extra attractions are offset by repulsions; it comes from a fall in the electrons' kinetic energy when they spread over a larger region instead of staying close to one nucleus.

paragraphs.heading: Covalent bonds
paragraphs.text: Picture a covalent bond at its simplest: one or more electrons, often a pair, are drawn into the space between two nuclei. Such a bond joins two particular atoms and points in a set direction, which is why drawings show it as a line and models show it as a stick between balls. When the electrons are shared unequally, the bond is called polar. Covalent bonds often build small, well-connected groups of atoms called molecules. In solids and liquids these molecules hold onto each other only through much weaker forces, which is why waxes and oils are soft and melt at low temperatures.

paragraphs.heading: Chains and networks
paragraphs.text: Covalent bonds can also link atoms into long chains, as in nylon, or run as networks through a whole solid, as in diamond and quartz. The result can then be both strong and tough. Such polymers and networks also melt at much higher temperatures.

paragraphs.heading: Ionic bonds
paragraphs.text: In a simple picture of an ionic bond, an electron is handed over rather than shared. One nucleus offers the electron a more tightly held place than the other, so one atom can pass an electron to its neighbour. That leaves one atom with a net positive charge and the other with a net negative charge, and the two charged particles, called ions, attract each other. Ionic bonds are strong, so these substances need high temperatures to melt, but they are brittle because the forces between ions reach only a short way. Crystals of table salt get their character from this kind of bond.

paragraphs.heading: Metallic bonds
paragraphs.text: In a metal, each atom gives one or more electrons to a shared sea of electrons lying among many atoms. Each of these electrons can be linked with a great many atoms at once. The atoms, left somewhat positive, stay bound because the loose electrons are attracted to all of them. This bonding is often very strong, which gives metals their tensile strength, yet the atoms are not held in fixed directions, so metal crystals deform more easily and metals are malleable. The same electron cloud explains why metals conduct electricity and heat well and look shiny.
